lesson.title: Wi-Fi: The Brand Name Behind 802.11
lesson.summary: Wi-Fi is the certified brand name for wireless LANs built on the IEEE 802.11 family of standards, and each new generation trades new frequency bands and radio techniques for higher speed and better efficiency.
lesson.body:
A wireless LAN only becomes useful at scale if a laptop from one manufacturer can reliably talk to an access point from a completely different one. That kind of interoperability does not happen by accident; it requires a shared, published technical specification that every vendor implements the same way. The IEEE, the same standards body responsible for Ethernet, publishes that specification for wireless LANs under the number 802.11, and the Wi-Fi Alliance, an industry consortium, tests products against it and grants them the Wi-Fi trademark when they pass certification.

Despite common belief, Wi-Fi is not an acronym for wireless fidelity; it is simply a brand name chosen to be catchy and easy to say, sitting on top of the underlying IEEE 802.11 standard. The 802.11 family defines exactly the pieces a wireless LAN needs to function: which frequency bands to use, how bits get modulated onto radio waves, and how the CSMA collision avoidance approach from the wireless LAN concept is actually implemented in practice.

Since the original 802.11 standard shipped in 1997, the family has grown through many amendments, each pushing more data through the air. 802.11b, from 1999, and 802.11g, from 2003, worked in the crowded 2.4 GHz band at up to 11 and 54 Mbps respectively. 802.11a, also 1999, moved to the roomier 5 GHz band at up to 54 Mbps. 802.11n, marketed later as Wi-Fi 4, added multiple antenna streams across both bands. 802.11ac, Wi-Fi 5, pushed further into 5 GHz with wider channels and multi-user antenna techniques. 802.11ax, Wi-Fi 6, and its 6 GHz sibling Wi-Fi 6E, focused on efficiency in dense, crowded environments as much as raw speed, and 802.11be, Wi-Fi 7, is the newest generation. The Wi-Fi Alliance introduced the simpler Wi-Fi 4, 5, 6, 7 numbering in 2018 precisely because the older 802.11 letter names had become confusing to ordinary consumers.

Suppose a household buys a new router advertised as Wi-Fi 6 while still owning an older laptop that only supports 802.11n, Wi-Fi 4. Both devices speak the same underlying 802.11 protocol family, so they can still associate and communicate; the connection simply falls back to the older, slower data rates and features that both ends actually support, rather than failing outright. That same router typically still advertises both the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands at once, letting the aging laptop join whichever band and generation it understands while a newer phone in the same house negotiates the faster Wi-Fi 6 features on the same access point. That backward compatibility, and the ability of one access point to serve a mix of old and new client devices at once, is a direct payoff of building Wi-Fi as an evolving standard rather than a series of incompatible proprietary systems.

Every concept that follows, access points, SSIDs, service sets, channels, and the RTS/CTS handshake, describes a specific piece of what the IEEE 802.11 standard defines and what Wi-Fi certification guarantees will behave the same way across vendors.
